author: Jacob Steinberg at the Gtech Community Stadium
description:
It was a record-breaking occasion in more ways than one. David Moyes made history for Everton, edging clear of Harry Catterick by overseeing his 593rd game in charge of the club, but calamitous defending ruined the Scot’s evening and defeat to Brentford was inevitable after James Tarkowski received his first red card in 351 Premier League appearances.

Those in Tarkowski’s corner will claim the Everton captain’s tackle on Yehor Yarmoliuk might not even have been given as a foul back in the day. This, though, was not a “game’s gone” moment. “He’s not that sort of player,” is not something anyone will ever say about Tarkowski. The defender’s back catalogue features plenty of orange card tackles and there was always likely to come a time when his luck ran out.

Continue reading...
title: Lewis-Potter double and Janelt stunner ease Brentford past 10-man Everton

author: Lucy Mangan
description:
The brilliant historian has a gift for cheering everybody up. In this series, she discovers the delights of European castles – and makes you want to spontaneously book a holiday

When I think of Lucy Worsley, I am immediately cheered up. Partly it’s the coats. (So neat! So bright! So wonder where she gets them and if I could carry one off!) Partly it’s the hairclips. (How big has she gone this time? Is it going to stay in?) But mostly it is her; her energy, her indefatigability, her determination to impart what she knows in the most accessible way and, above all, her abundant confidence without ego. It’s the latter that allows for that rare thing – other historians to be interviewed and share their knowledge with the lay person at home without the presenter champing at the bit to show that he or she knows this already and that they are just letting them simplify things for the good of the show. This is my personal bugbear, so thank you for letting me exorcise it here, and tha
title: Lucy Worsley’s Keys to the Castle review – heavenly TV that instantly brightens up your day

author: Associated Press
description:
Three-judge panel reverses order of keeping case in state court, allowing president to seek dismissal on immunity grounds

A federal appeals court on Monday gave Donald Trump a new pathway to erasing his hush money criminal conviction, moving the case to a federal court where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds.

A three-judge panel of the second US circuit court of appeals reversed a lower court decision that had kept the case in state court in New York, where Trump was tried and convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult-film performer Stormy Daniels.

Continue reading...
title: Federal appeals court hands Trump way out of conviction for hush-money payment

author: Suzanne Wrack
description:
Maximising the societal impact of the tournament, especially combating misogyny, should be a top priority

The announcement that the 2035 Women’s World Cup will be hosted in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland has finally come and, if we aim high enough, it could have a massive societal impact.

Confirmation was a foregone conclusion – the UK was the only bidder – but that did not mean the submission was complacent or lacked ambition.

Continue reading...
title: The 2035 Women’s World Cup has huge potential for women and girls in UK

author: Adrian Horton
description:
The Summer I Turned Pretty’s Christopher Briney and 1923’s Michelle Randolph try their best, but this chaotic cross-country journey is not worth taking

Credit where credit is due: it takes some nerve for Amazon to open its latest holiday romcom, Clashing Through the Snow, with characters bemoaning the enervated state of the book industry. Publishing isn’t the cultural epicenter it once was, reports boutique press head Jeremy (PJ Byrne) before announcing some impending new year’s layoffs. Alas, things have changed – “if Faulkner were alive today, he’d be making ASMR videos with Mr Beast” (or, perhaps, competing on Prime Video’s Beast Games?)

Self-awareness can be key to the ludicrous joys of a Christmas romcom confection, though Clashing Through the Snow, starring 1923’s Michelle Randolph and homegrown Amazon star Christopher Briney (The Summer I Turned Pretty), tests one’s patience for beating you to the branded punchline. An Iranian singer and four members of her production team ⁠have each received 74 lashes after being sentenced for “offending public decency by producing and ⁠publishing obscene and ⁠immoral ​content online”, an Iranian news website said on Monday.

London force also makes eight arrests in operation centred on New Spitalfields Market in the capital

A tonne of cocaine was found hidden in boxes of oranges as part of one of the biggest drug seizures in the history of the Metropolitan police.

Suspected cocaine weighing 893kg has been seized and eight arrests made as part of the investigation that targeted an organised crime group alleged to have been smuggling class A drugs into the UK. A Met spokesperson said the investigation was continuing.

Mahdi Tounsi appeared with visible bruising after being interrogated by police on his association with Israeli-Palestinian organisations

Israeli professors, students and rights activists are calling for the immediate release of Mahdi Tounsi, a sociology student at Jerusalem’s Hebrew University who has been held without charge for more than two weeks after he was seized from his dorm room.

The detention comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.

Environmentalists sued last week to stop detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide over health and pollution concerns

Donald Trump on Monday said he would defer to a federal appeals court on whether the administration moves ahead with plans to detonate several tons of degraded bomb-making material at an Iowa ammunition plant.

Nearly 400 people live in Middletown, where the plant is sited, and thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground.

author: Editorial
description:
Petrostates blocked ambition while wealthy nations withheld cash support. The climate crisis demands the next UN summit turns promises into action

In a negotiation the maxim is usually that no deal is better than a bad deal. But the failure of Cop31 in Turkey to get a climate pact – the first time this has happened in 17 years – should not be an excuse for leaving the planet with the damaging status quo. A hard bargain needs a credible route to agreement: by making commitments, seeking concessions and getting others to reciprocate. This did not happen at the weekend.

Responsibility for the breakdown lay principally with petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels and wealthy nations that are unwilling to finance it properly. With the US absent, the EU was foremost among the latter. European governments’ objection to fossil-
title: The Guardian view on Cop31: a just transition needs more than fine words | Editorial

author: Editorial
description:
On treacherous political terrain, the government is right to want to proceed with caution and at a pace of its own choosing

During the 1980s and 90s, the French president of the European Commission, Jacques Delors, consciously pursued deeper EU integration via a gradualist approach that sought to minimise confrontation. Rather than focusing on ambitious end-goals, risking a showdown with some member states, Delors calculated that taking steps such as the creation of the internal market, in 1993, would eventually generate the momentum to go further. One thing would lead to another, in a logic of deeper union.

Nebahat Isbilen claims her former adviser paid bribe in return for help with passport, but money was returned

Nebahat Isbilen is suing her former adviser, businessman Selman Turk, over allegations he misappropriated tens of millions of pounds of her funds.

description:
Burning the midnight oil playing video games is not ideal preparation for professional sport – but it’s not all bad

“They miss games, the check’s still clearing. And you’re trying to tell me they got this kind of addiction to a video game that they sitting there with their thumbs looking like Donald Trump?” That was EPSN’s Stephen A Smith, one of the US’s most provocative and influential sports pundits, spitting fire and fury last week after hearing that so many NBA and NFL stars were absorbed in Grand Theft Auto VI.

Smith was hardly an outlier. Other pundits, as well as some Manchester United fans, also questioned Bryan Mbeumo’s focus and professionalism after he posted an image of GTA VI and the word “historique” after midnight on Thursday.

French woman says she will pursue legal action against publisher and author over use of photos taken by convicted husband

Gisèle Pelicot has said she is “deeply shocked” that nude photographs of her had been used without her consent to promote a psychoanalyst’s book that suggests she was complicit in her abuse.

Pelicot, 73, became a global icon in the fight against sexual violence in 2024 during the trial that saw her former husband convicted of drugging and raping her, as well as recruiting 49 other men to rape her while unconscious.

There are only six beds specifically for trans victims of domestic abuse in the UK, a new report has found, with services saying it is “almost impossible” to find refuges for trans people since the supreme court ruling on single-sex spaces.

Galop, an LGBTQ+ anti-abuse charity, called on the government to create an emergency national fund for specialist trans refuges, as many were being turned away from mainstream services.

title: Only six beds for trans victims of domestic abuse in UK, report finds

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to an article by Rafael Behr on the Shenzhen summit, where the three world leaders met without a place at the table for Europe

Rafael Behr (Trump, Xi and Putin have a shared vision of global power – with no place for Europe, 18 November) draws parallels between the Shenzhen summit and Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin and Franklin D Roosevelt meeting at Yalta. I see it as bringing us a step closer to George Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four, in which the world is divided into three superstates: Oceania, Eurasia and Eastasia.

We already have the surveillance in the form of CCTV, facial-recognition technology and email trawling. Daily we witness the rewriting of history. We could be sleepwalking into a situation from which we will be unable to escape.
Andy Fazakerley
Irby, Wirral

description:
Historian who transformed the understanding of empire and its role in shaping modern societies

How does ruling the world change the rulers themselves? If such a question has become self-evident today, it was not the case in 1984, when John M MacKenzie, who has died aged 82, published Propaganda and Empire: The Manipulation of British Public Opinion, 1880-1960.

Through his analysis of a wide range of cultural artefacts, until then neglected by historians, he articulated some of the key questions that would structure the “imperial turn”. Rivals have been heading in opposite directions in recent years but latest clash showed some things never change

It was late, it was lucky, and there wasn’t even a winner but right there, right then, at 24 minutes past 8pm on Saturday evening in the Ramón Sánchez-Pizjuán Stadium, it felt like there was. Frankly it was a bit rubbish, as bad a goal as you’ll see, but it was also the best, practically Pelé against the Nazis. Suddenly there were arms and legs everywhere, tears too. Cameras confirmed it. Zoom in and there they are: actual, real life tears.

Over-18s in Britain: share your thoughts on why young and middle-aged people are having sex less frequently than in the past

The UK is experiencing a “relationship recession”, according to a report published this month by the Centre for Social Justice thinktank.

Latest greyhound racing blow is a wake-up call with new five-year plan keeping RSPCA on side for now

Britain’s greyhound racing industry woke up on Monday to the news that the Racing Post, the daily trade newspaper that has carried extensive coverage of the sport since its launch in 1986, will drop both editorial and greyhound racecards in its print edition from 10 December.

In a letter to Racing Post readers, Tom Kerr, its editor, said that it had been an “immensely difficult decision” and blamed “tax rises that have hit betting shops [which] have put pressure on the whole industry,” adding that “like other businesses, we have to make hard choices about where we focus our resources.” Five members of staff are expected to lose their jobs as a result of the decision.

Grounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly.

Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure.

author: Nadia Khomami

The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one

“Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own.

Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. Centred around the world premiere of jazz bassist Misha Mullov-Abbado’s almost-concerto, the tight ensemble took a tour of classical fusion and tango fisticuffs

In this eclectic programme of mostly 21st-century music, the United Strings of Europe found the intersection in a Venn diagram of chamber music, string orchestra and jazz. description:
With Musk, NAZA and You Can See Everything finding large audiences, non-fiction cinema is poised to break through. But there are plenty more gripping stories waiting for their turn in the spotlight

There comes a time in the life of every film enthusiast when they must set aside foolish fictions and face up to some hard truths. Specifically, that time arrives each November in the form of the International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA for short), with its tales of crisis and strife, angry resistance and everyday human kindness. The world’s largest documentary festival plays out in the city’s twinkling downtown district, quite near the torture museum, and provides a sharp corrective to the confected dramas and A-list pageantry of Cannes, Toronto and Venice. author: Ben Fisher in Istanbul
description:
• ‘Hopefully the pitch will be as best as possible,’ says Villa manager

  • Turkish champions had to move game on Saturday

Unai Emery has insisted he will not alter his plans for Aston Villa’s Champions Leaguegame at Galatasaray on Tuesday night on account of concerns about the state of the pitch. The Turkish champions hastily moved Saturday’s home fixture from Rams Park after starting emergency repairs to the surface this month. Galatasaray played Saturday’s victory over Samsunspor at Basaksehir Fatih Terim stadium, a significantly smaller ground named after the former Turkey manager, who played for and managed Galatasaray.

author: Annilese Miskimmon
description:
The death and pain of female characters has always been a bedrock of opera. Kaija Saariaho and today’s female composers are challenging this narrative, and thereby connecting with today’s world

In 1992, the Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho saw a Salzburg festival production of Messiaen’s Saint François d’Assise. A series of meditative theological tableaux in which naturalism and plot is secondary to the revelation of deeper spiritual truths, it is now hailed as a masterpiece although it divided critics on its Paris premiere in 1983.

Saariaho, one of the painfully few female composers in opera’s 400-year history, recalled thinking: “If that is an opera, then I can write one”. And she did, to notable international acclaim. Her first opera L’Amour de loin (Love from Afar), a tale of medieval courtly love with a libretto by war correspondent and writer Amin Maalouf was premiered, appropriately, at 2000’s Salzburg festival and came to the U
title: Saariaho’s Adriana Mater transcends horror for hope. Female composers are rejecting opera’s legacy of violence | Annilese Miskimmon

Jurors hear Anthony Russell killed Soham murderer by hitting him repeatedly over head with metal bar

A prisoner killed the Soham murderer Ian Huntley with a heavy metal bar in a “cold-blooded” attack that had been planned weeks in advance, a court heard.

Jurors were told that Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly hit the 52-year-old over the head in the attack at the high-security HMP Frankland, near Durham.

author: Luke Entwistle
description:
Désiré Doué sustained an ACL injury in PSG’s 3-2 win at Nice and joins Khvicha Kvaratskhelia on the treatment table

By Get French Football News

Luis Enrique is in uncharted territory, even if he insists that “it isn’t a first”. Since arriving at Paris Saint-Germain in 2023, only three players have spent more than 100 days on the sideline – Nuno Mendes, Lucas Hernandez and Presnel Kimpembe – and only Mendes is an important first-team player. But for the remainder of the season, or at least the vast majority of it, Luis Enrique must do without two of his stars: Désiré Doué and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

author: Photography by Charles Brooks, words by Emma Joyce
description:
Photographer and former cellist Charles Brooks creates optical illusions with minuscule cameras. He threads endoscopes inside instruments to capture thousands of images which are then combined: a clarinet becomes a dark tunnel, a yidaki becomes a cave, a Steinway piano is a futuristic train station: ‘You’re also looking inside the history of these instruments … All the marks you’re seeing are from them being cleaned or repaired, or by the maker themselves’

One of Australia’s greatest tennis players remembers being pelted with coins, tampering with nets and wanting to ‘beat these fuckers’

This year’s Davis Cup Finals begin in Bologna on Tuesday but the culmination of the oldest team competition in tennis will probably pass most Australian sports fans by.

Fans at concert where unknown substance was released into crowd tell of ‘shocking’ checks and ticketless people ‘hopping barriers’

Concertgoers in Manchester have criticised an “atrocious” lack of security at the Co-op Live arena after an unknown substance released into the crowd left fans “screaming for help” and caused thousands to be evacuated.

author: Brian Logan
description:
Royal & Derngate, Northampton
The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties

Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake.

Cabbage will always be a top-tier vegetable in my eyes – it’s so versatile, from braising to roasting, from shredding it into a fritter to slowly cooking into a soup. I love it! Shortly after this year’s London book fair, rumours began to circulate of a seven-figure book deal for a rewrite of the wildly popular work of Harry Potter fan fiction All the Young Dudes. First published between 2017 and 2018 by user MsKingBean89 on the online platform Archive of Our Own, All the Young Dudes is arguably the most-read work of fan fiction of all time. Now it will be repackaged as a series under the pen name BN King, with the first novel, Wolfboy, due to be published in autumn 2027.

author: Jayni Makwana
description:
Four-year-old me had never worried about fashion fails or making a fool of myself. It was time to ditch this grown-up obsession with getting everything right

As a student, I have spent months worrying about assignments long after submitting them, and criticised myself over tiny things such as making spelling mistakes in birthday cards. author: Sarah Johnson in Mangabe reserve, Madagascar
description:

As Albert Rakotoarisoa emerges from the forest into a clearing in Mangabe reserve in the east of Madagascar, he sees dozens of holes dug in the marshy ground, a sign that people have been here to search for gold.

author: Matt Hughes in Zurich

Price plunges 67% as Adolfo Hernandez leaves with ‘immediate effect’ amid continued fallout from pension payment problems

The boss of troubled outsourcing group Capita has abruptly departed as he admitted it has “not delivered” for retired civil servants left waiting for pension payments.

Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm’s board to step down with “immediate effect”, it said on Monday. He will be replaced by chief financial officer Pablo Andres for the top job.

author: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent
description:
Future of familiar school-run figures uncertain as vacancies surge and town halls consider alternatives

They have been a feature of British schooldays for decades, instantly recognisable by their round signs and yellow hi-vis uniforms. But a struggle to recruit against a backdrop of staff cuts at cash-strapped local authorities is threatening to make lollipop people a thing of the past.

The Recruitment and Employment Confederation (REC) said school crossing patrols were among jobs showing the biggest increase in vacancies in recent weeks, alongside sales roles and exam invigilators.

Continue reading...
title: Fears for school crossing patrols as councils struggle to recruit lollipop people

author: Ashleigh Arnott
description:
As we come to the end of another series, former contestants including Kim-Joy, Syabira Yusoff and Christiaan de Vries reminisce on their time in the tent – and the aftermath

The Great British Bake Off is just about to finish its best season in years. Like a cloud of Swiss meringue buttercream on a slightly sunken cake, Nigella Lawson has added glamour and indulgence to a format that needed saving. But this year’s contestants have brought the joy, too: talented, charismatic individuals who have interrupted their lives to spend three months with bits of dough stuck to their elbows and indigestion from all the recipe testing.

We spoke to five previous contestants to find out why they put themselves through it, and what they feel they achieved in the process. The scale runs from “a very nice level of X-list celebrity” to “a better version of me”, with a lot of life lessons (and a fart corner) along the way.
title: ‘One area of the tent was known as fart corner’: what it’s really like to be on The Great British Bake Off

author: Morgan Jerkins
description:
The latest in our series of writers picking their most rewatched comfort films is an ode to Eddie Murphy’s beloved culture-clash comedy

“Good morning, my neighbors!” A young Eddie Murphy shouts from the balcony of a shady apartment building. In the bustling Queens neighborhood, he sticks out like a sore thumb with his foreign accent, tailored blazing jacket and red tie. “Hey, fuck you!” A voice yells from below and Murphy repeats the phrase, believing that it’s a greeting rather than an insult. It’s one of the standout scenes from the film Coming to America, because it’s so absurd but effective in that there is a cultural clash going on here.

In Coming to America, Prince Akeem, played by Eddie Murphy, is the sole heir to the throne of Zamunda, a fictitious African country. Instead of having an arranged marriage, Prince Akeem exercises his autonomy and intends to find his own bride somewhere far away from the continent, much to his parents’ chagrin. With the coin-flip an
title: ‘Reminds me of home’: why Coming to America is my feelgood movie

author: Peter Bradshaw
description:
Nicolas Wadimoff invites refugees to draw a floor plan of their former neighbourhood, bringing raw and agonising pain to the surface

A sombre documentary from the Swiss musician and film-maker Nicolas Wadimoff, who returns to his longstanding interest in Gaza. In this film, a group of survivor-refugees who made it out of Gaza and into Egypt during the bombing gather in an enclosed studio and are invited to draw out a kind of floor plan of what they remember of their neighbourhood. First, this is on paper and then on the studio floor itself; they use that as a basis for their memories of what and who they have lost. (The people who have died are described as having been “martyred”.)

The result is almost unbearably painful. The raw and agonising grief, which perhaps stays just at the waterline of consciousness most of the time, is here brought above the surface. They are people suffering from trauma, carrying videos on their phones of their lost loved ones. One interviewe
title: Who Is Still Alive review – grief-stricken stories of the places and people lost in Gaza

author: Chloe Mac Donnell
description:
Culinary artists are turning fashion shows and design fairs into a feast for the eyes

A pretty Venetian chandelier featuring delicate pink flowers and cascading blue leaves hangs from a ceiling. A hazy, warm light radiates from its tulip bulbs. Suddenly, a woman reaches up and snaps off one of the flower stems, giggling as she begins to nibble it. Welcome to the weird and wonderful world of Laila Gohar. The Egyptian-born, New York-based artist is part of a new wave of culinary artists blurring the lines between sustenance and spectacle, and this troupe have quickly become a firm fixture at fashion parties and design fairs, turning dining into a phenomenon and delight.

Gohar describes the chandelier, made entirely from hand-spun sugar (including the silver chain that suspended it) as her “favourite thing she has done in recent history”. It joins a long list of extravagant y
title: Brioche armchairs, butter sculptures and edible chandeliers: meet the new food artists

author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
description:
Experts say ruling closing ‘incoherent gap’ has implications for countries such as UK and Germany over arming Israel

Countries could be found in breach of the duty to prevent genocide even if it is ultimately determined that the legal threshold for genocide has not been met, the international court of justice has declared.

The ruling, described as a major legal development, has implications for third parties such as the UK and Germany as they face legal and political scrutiny over their arming of Israel.

Continue reading...
title: ICJ ruling on duty to prevent genocide places new onus on countries to act

author: Andrew Sparrow
description:
PM expected to tell Commons that Friday’s deal will be ‘the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament’

Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, has declined to say whether Natural England will be abolished as part of plans to cut the number of quangos.

In a story in the Times today, Patrick Maguire says:

The Times has been told that proposals for greater public control, due to be announced next month in Burnham’s ten-year plan for government, will include cuts to the arms-length bodies Haigh blames for planning delays, pollution and high energy costs.

Natural England, the environment regulator, could be among the casualties. Senior ministers believe it is obstructing government plans to build hundreds of thousands of homes, piling unnecessary costs onto developers and preventing the
title: Andy Burnham to give update to MPs after ‘landmark’ UK-EU summit – UK politics live

author: Alexis Petridis
description:
The rock critic’s obsessive yet incisive sorting of musical genius is a contrarian delight

As veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along.

The NME got there first, in 1974, with what it called a “Writers’ All-Time Top 100 Albums” list – a bold early attempt to define a canon of classic
title: Bill Wyman’s Rock & Roll Lists review – greatest hits and biggest misses

author: Jakub Krupa
description:
President says Kyiv responsible for sinking Merkury warship in Benghazi on Sunday and also drone attack on cargo vessel MV Angara

Zelenskyy also said that “partners” – presumably the US – want the fourway talks between Ukraine, Russia, the US and Europe to take place before Christmas.

description:
First secretary of state says proliferation of arms-length government bodies is hampering decision-making

The nature watchdog Natural England could be abolished as part of a cull of arm’s length government organisations, Louise Haigh has said.

Saying that the proliferation of quangos and other similar bodies had made decision-making by ministers more difficult, the first secretary of state said it could fall within a push to change the landscape of government by scrapping some organisations and bringing others into departments.

Continue reading...
title: Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh

author: Ruth Gilligan
description:
A real-life flooding becomes a flashpoint in this novel exploring family relationships, female liberation and the drive for Welsh independence

In the author’s note accompanying her eighth novel, Adder Stone, Clare Clark recalls first learning how a lake in the Welsh valleys shrank during the drought of 1976 only to reveal an abandoned village underneath. As a child, Clark became obsessed with the idea, envisaging a sort of Welsh Pompeii – houses and lives frozen in time, buried beneath the water and the mud.

Fifty years since that uncanny occurrence, Clark’s richly researched novel seeks to tell the story of that forgotten Welsh village: not abandoned by choice, but forcibly evicted in order to make way for a new reservoir needed to service Liverpool’s growing population. Clark charts how this event had a profound impact on individual lives, but also how it served as a flashpoint in the broader conversation around Welsh independence.
title: Adder Stone by Clare Clark review – the story of a drowned Welsh village

author: Lauren Almeida
description:
Jump in price follows slowdown in Qatar supplies and depleted summer stocks due to heatwaves

  • Business live – latest updates

European gas prices surged on Monday as a forecast cold snap in the coming weeks fed fears across the continent’s over depleted supply this winter and costly household bills.

The Dutch month-ahead contract – the European benchmark for gas prices over the next four weeks – rose by as much as 8.6% to €96.08, before settling up 4% at €92.50.

Continue reading...
title: Gas prices in Europe surge as forecast cold snap feeds supply shortage fears

author: Melissa Jacobs
description:
Baltimore have been one of the most successful teams in the league this century. But recent events have dinged their reputation

The Baltimore Ravens have lost in all sorts of fashion in recent weeks. There were the blowout losses to juggernauts Buffalo, Jacksonville, and Cincinnati. There was the nailbiting divisional loss to Cleveland. There was the embarrassing defeat to the previously winless Chargers. But Sunday’s 35-33 loss to Carolina, the team’s sixth straight, hit different.

Sunday was a massive test. Did Baltimore have the fortitude to bounce back and stay alive in the AFC North, with the hope of getting the injured Lamar Jackson back at some point? Almost.

author: Robert Kitson
description:
France have the chance to topple the Springboks in the Nations Championship decider, with their Six Nations rivals also shining this autumn

Even if the official November Test window had now closed, as used to be the case, this would already have been a vintage European autumn. Whatever still awaits on the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend, it has been a richly enjoyable few weeks for both diehard fans and floating voters, topped off by more seismic results and overflowing emotions in London and Dublin on Saturday.

Those flocking to Twickenham had their money’s worth even before the game started, as Lewis Moody, fighting the good fight against motor neurone disease, stood shoulder to shoulder with England’s players as they faced up to the All Blacks’ haka. A r
title: England and Ireland provide champagne rugby for north to tee up finals weekend | Robert Kitson

author: Andy Hunter
description:
Everton striker has worked hard to find his scoring touch after admitting he hit ‘rock bottom’ at times last season

A most unexpected name sits behind the phenomenon Erling Haaland and the £125m proven marksman Alexander Isak in the Premier League goalscoring chart this season. The rise of Thierno Barry may have surprised even the man himself but stands as a fitting reward for single-minded perseverance and the refusal to quit.

“Fabulous” was David Moyes’s take on Barry’s last performance for Everton, when a double against Coventry took the striker to 10 goals for the season in all competitions and his team temporarily up to fifth. It was high praise indeed from a manager who does not dispense tributes freely, and can appear to be on the French forward’s case constantly, but was no more than Barry deserved for a display that also featured an assist for Everton’s t
title: ‘Haaland must be worried’: Thierno Barry’s rise has David Moyes purring

author: Graeme Green
description:
After some satirical experiments with the ‘disgusting’ AI, the photographer has returned to his first love with a book of contact sheets from his celebrity shoots. ‘I wish we could go back and stop everything changing,’ he says

“I hate AI,” says Rankin. “A lot of people think I’m an evangelical twat about it, and I’m not. I think it’s disgusting. I think the people who run it are disgusting. They’ve made a massive gamble with humanity and society and culture.”

His contempt may surprise anyone who’s familiar with Rankin’s substantial AI output. Ever since the artist Damien Hirst introduced him to the possibilities of generative AI in 2021, the British photographer has been going further down the rabbit hole. “I’m not somebody who likes to be critical about something without actually knowing about it,” he explains. “I’ve gone deep into trying to work it out.”
title: Dapper Liam and Noel, experimental Björk, and Bowie ‘cuddling himself’: Rankin reveals his never-before-seen shots of the stars

author: Guardian sport
description:
Leeds offer Chelsea a lesson, Newcastle’s summer recruits struggle and Jules Ahoka makes a name for himself

What to make of Manchester United’s utterly torrid start under Mauricio Pochettino? To go glass half full as the new head coach had only three days to prepare the side for the trip to Anfield, the hope will be that time will cast the 4-0 humbling from Liverpool as the falsest of false starts. The glass-half-empty scenario, though, is that here was an XI packed with internationals that had zero clue how to sort out a dire beginning themselves. description:
A step or a jump

Today’s puzzle is about the hidden mathematical pattern behind a much-loved video game.

Consider a simplified game of Super Mario. He moves from platform to platform. He can either step forward 1 space, to the next platform, or jump forward 2 spaces, to the platform after that.

3 platforms?

4 platforms?

5 platforms?

10 platforms?

title: Can you solve it? How Super Mario explains Renaissance art

description:
MPs to discuss bereavement support as financial help for funeral expenses and bereaved families fails to keep pace with costs

Bereaved families are borrowing money or forgoing a service with mourners because financial help available from the state no longer covers even half a typical funeral director’s fee.

“The funeral expenses payment (FSP) was originally meant to cover the cost of a simple funeral. Today, that is a pipe dream,” said Lindesay Mace, a co-manager of Down to Earth, a funeral costs support service run by the charity Quaker Social Action.

author: Helen Pilcher
description:
Women of my age have been training for this job for years – solving problems, defusing tensions, keeping everyone fed – and we absolutely smash it

Nasa is hiring and I’m over the moon. The US space agency is recruiting its next cohort of astronauts to work on the lunar surface and “help write the next chapter of humanity’s greatest adventure”. Applications close on 3 December.

This isn’t the only job I’ve been swooning over lately. I can’t tell you how many hours I’ve lost to posts about deliciously distant jobs: running the world’s southernmost post office in Antarctica, where staff double as penguin counters, or
title: Nasa, please send me to the moon. Science says I’m the perfect crew member | Helen Pilcher

author: Phil Hoad
description:
Encouraged by his grandfather and single mother, the teen Borja dreams of a career that will end his family’s poverty, but the protesters are gathering strength

Where last year’s bullfighting documentary Afternoons of Solitude by Albert Serra was a tightly trussed formalistic affair concerned by the question of style in the arena and in art, this Scottish-produced film is a looser, more social-realist approach to la corrida. Swerving a portrayal of the butchery itself, it focuses on the wider community significance of this tradition in the eastern Spanish city of Castellón, via the figure of aspiring teen toreador Borja.

Supported by his harried, cigarillo-smoking single mother, Raquel, Borja hopes that wearing the sequined “suit of lights” will help lift his family out of poverty. Everything in his vicinity seems to point
title: The Boy and the Suit of Lights review – a sensitive portrait of an aspiring toreador in a changing Spain

author: Paul Sullivan
description:
The cold is legendary, but there’s hot chocolate and Glühwein to warm you up, plus crowd-free museums and galleries and cosy candlelit pubs

One of the first things Berliners warned me about when I moved here in 2008 was the winters. They talked in hushed, conspiratorial tones about the harsh winds that blew in from the Russian steppes, temperatures of minus 15C and the horrors of frozen bike locks. Having survived 17 of these winters (and counting), and still no hospitalisations for frostbite to report, I can confirm that the warnings, although not necessarily untrue, are not the whole story.

Although some Berlin winter days are cold, miserable and grey, they can also be charming, cheerful and chock-full of possibilities. No sooner has the temperature dropped, and the last yellow leaves see-sawed from the trees at the end of November, than the city’s Christmas markets assert themselves in a blaze of tw
title: Why I love Berlin in winter: ‘Christmas markets arrive in a blaze of twinkling lights’

author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
description:
The folding iPhone is early-adopter gold, changing the way iOS works and successfully condensing a tablet into your pocket, but it is not for everyone

Apple’s first folding phone has upended the usual order of things with some interesting choices about how you use a iPhone – for better or worse.

The Duo sits atop the pile as Apple’s most expensive smartphone – at £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,499) it costs more than most of its folding Android rivals and as much as the iPhone 18 Pro Max and the latest iPad mini combined.

Continue reading...
title: Apple iPhone Duo review: the most novel and interesting iPhone in almost a decade

author: Anna Gordon
description:
Anna Gordon met hospice care workers across the UK, learning how dignity and choice help create meaningful moments for patients

Most people in the UK actively avoid conversations about death and dying. They can be visibly uncomfortable when you raise the subject. When people try to talk about it, it tends to be euphemistically.

This is a mistake, one that can stop you from making important choices for yourself or your loved ones. It can increase fear and misunderstanding about what death can look like, while open conversations can help to ease these feelings and bring a sense of calm, peace and, on occasion, even beauty to the event.

Jenna Heritage: ‘Everyone’s big fear is that they are going to die in pain’

Rachel Aroesti

Andy Burnham is not backtracking or delaying his ambitions to create even closer links with the EU in the wake of a landmark summit in Brussels, the Guardian has been told, after signs of an apparent slowdown in the timetable.

author: Joanna Partridge
description:
Rents to rise by 14% until at least 2029, Hamptons predicts, as high demand for properties and low supply push up costs for tenants

The cost of renting a home in Britain is expected to rise about twice as fast as that of buying one until at least 2029, according to research, with shrinking supply pushing up the prices paid by tenants.

Rents on newly agreed lets are forecast to grow by 14.2% between 2026 and 2029, compared with house price growth of 7.2%, according to forecasts from estate agent Hamptons.

author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
description:
Looking after my brother when I was a child was challenging and life-affirming. Now we need to give the next generation of carers proper support

As the years have passed, I have often observed that caring for another person is a responsibility that few human beings completely escape. “Hardly anyone gets off scot-free in this life,” I recently said to a friend, as we discussed our various loved ones and their care needs, the worry and the responsibilities. Whether it’s our children, siblings, friends or parents, some sort of care work is usually required of us on our life’s journey. Illness, disability, mental health issues, ageing, accidents and other vulnerabilities inevitably touch our lives.

There are 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, but I suspect there are far more who don’t identify as such, yet regularly care for loved ones or neighbours

author: Soledad Dominguez in Buenos Aires
description:
While Argentina and the UK dispute sovereignty over the islands and its vast oil reserves, environmentalists fear for one of the Atlantic’s richest ecosystems

From the air, the main Falkland Islands form two large, jagged shapes against the South Atlantic. East Falkland and West Falkland are surrounded by 778 smaller islands and islets east of Patagonia’s southern tip.

The archipelago, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, is home to large colonies of albatrosses and penguins. Its waters, with those of the Patagonian shelf, provide feeding grounds for sea lions, southern elephant seals and southern right whales.

Continue reading...

author: Alessandro Giannatempo
description:
Sweet from top to toe: a creamy, southern Italian fruit and nut cake, and an almondy polenta porridge from the north

Although I grew up in Emilia-Romagna, my family history spans the Italian peninsula. Inspired by my mixed upbringing, these recipes reflect the flavours of both southern and northern Italy. The Amalfi-style ricotta and pear cake, as the name suggests, is a nod to the southern coast of Salerno. Fresh ricotta is whipped with lemony pears and sandwiched between layers of nutty hazelnut cake. The crocodile’s porridge, named after a traditional Italian beverage made with milk and pear juice, combines northern ingredients such as polenta and amaro for a very cosy stovetop-made dessert – or breakfast, if you ask me!

Ed Miliband is being urged by MPs to use his powers to force overseas territories such as the British Virgin Islands to publish public company ownership registers – almost a decade after parliament voted for transparency.

author: John Gilbey
description:
Cadair Idris, Gwynedd: Past golden hillsides and the great Cadair Idris, through wooded valleys, to the starting point for my walk

The morning starts bright but cold, with a hazy mist clinging to the trees across the valley. This could be one of the last good weather days, so I take the bus north into Gwynedd, clambering awkwardly upstairs to get the best view of the autumn colours.

The mist begins to clear and, in a wet meadow, a heron stands alertly by a ditch, watching for movement. Beyond the Afon Dyfi, the hills are golden with patches of larch and the deeper orange tones of the oak and ash. Well-defined shadows below the dark blue sky shelter pockets of still-frosted gloom, as we cross the Dyfi into Gwynedd.

Continue reading...

author: Michael Savage Media editor

Fewer than half of households in Britain will pay the BBC’s licence within a decade, according to analysis that warns that the broadcaster’s funding is locked in a “spiral of decline”.

Brussels rolled out a warm welcome for the PM but toxic UK politics around rejoining have not gone away

Despite the beaming smiles and the symbolic triple handshake, the summit intended to reset the UK’s tortured relationship with the EU showed just how difficult undoing Brexit will be a decade after Britons voted to leave.

To be sure, Brussels laid on a warm welcome. Andy Burnham’s first summit with the heads of the EU institutions felt like the homecoming of an old friend who had been away too long, rather than a meeting to settle some awkward leftovers of a bitter divorce.

Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

title: Undoing Brexit is the right thing to attempt – but sadly, I can't see Andy Burnham pulling it off | Paul Taylor

author: Philip Oltermann
description:
For decades, films about Nazi-occupied Europe were all about the fearless resistance while despicable collaborators deserved all they got. So what’s behind the spate of movies portraying turncoats in a more sympathetic light?

A young maid busies herself in a vast, high-ceilinged apartment, serving her master steaming coffee in fine china and polishing the hefty family silver, as she picks her way across the checkerboard parquet lit by stylish Poul Henningsen lamps. Woman Unknown, which won the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival this year, is set in the immediate aftermath of Denmark’s liberation from Nazi rule, but you wouldn’t know that from the opening scenes: five years of occupation, martial law and rationing have left the splendour of the Danish bourgeoisie miraculously untouched.

The trauma of wartime violence only comes rushing back in occasional burst
title: ‘What if joining the resistance got your friends executed?’ The chilling new films casting Nazi collaborators in a fresh light

author: Matthew Taylor
description:
Scientific and satellite findings warn of widespread contamination in Gaza, posing grave threats to public health ‘for generations to come’

Israel’s destruction of Gaza has left a devastating environmental legacy with poisoned water, contaminated soil and toxic air threatening the life-support systems that the population depends on for survival, according to a report.

Israel’s military assault has created widespread contamination across the entire strip, the report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (Ceobs) finds, with heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and sewage making the air, soil and water dangerous for Palestinians for decades to come.

title: Israel’s destruction of Gaza has created a ‘toxic wasteland’, experts find

The former South Africa batter was in the middle when Cameron Bancroft was caught by TV cameras using sandpaper in the third Test at Newlands in Cape Town.

author: Associated Press
description:
Army invokes emergency provisions in Iowa to avoid court order despite worries about health and environment risks

The US army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder.

“To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” government lawyers told the eight US circuit court of appeals in a filing late on Saturday. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”

Continue reading...
title: US army to blow up bomb-making chemicals despite safety concerns

Virginia dinner comes as Democrats accuse president of improperly profiting from his cryptocurrency ventures

Donald Trump is scheduled to headline his third cryptocurrency gala on ⁠Sunday night at his ​country club in Virginia, rewarding top holders of his own meme coin as Democrats accuse the president of improperly profiting from his crypto ventures.

The dinner, set to take place at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, will include meet-and-greets with Trump supporters including the boxing champion Floyd Mayweather, Shark Tank investor Kevin O’Leary, NBA champion Tristan Thompson and mentalist Lior Suchard, according to the event’s website.
title: Trump hosts third crypto gala for meme coin amid conflict of interest outcry

author: Jonathan Jones
description:
Hayward Gallery, London
The photographer finds echoes of Caravaggio and Greek myth in her erotic images, while her disturbing animal montages show that while humans can be beautiful, we are far from innocent

It’s the dirty realism of Nan Goldin’s images, her unfazed photography of the rough seams of spontaneous, dangerous lives, that enables her to create a film of such unlikely ambition as Stendhal Syndrome. This ecstatic condition is named after the French novelist who in 1817 fell ill in Florence, after gorging on the beauty of the Renaissance city’s treasures until “I had palpitations of the heart … I walked with the fear of falling”. Goldin, too, has suffered a bout of this aesthetic delirium, not in Italy but Paris – “the first time I was alone in the Louvre”, she explains on screen.

She infects you with it in a ravishing work housed in what looks like a bronze yurt entered via a vau
title: Cat’s whiskers: Nan Goldin proves that she’s the greatest US artist since Warhol – review
